title: Organizing Yourself to Delegate Effectively
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece diagnoses a common leadership failure: waiting until a distant deadline is suddenly close before realizing that early prep work should have been delegated weeks earlier. The author argues the root cause is disorganization, not lack of willingness to delegate, since leaders who are buried in urgent tasks never step back to map out what's coming next. The fix proposed is a simple three-tier task structure sorted by time horizon, which forces leaders to identify long-range work early enough to hand pieces of it off. The piece also notes a secondary cost of poor delegation planning: team members lose out on the growth and ownership that comes from being looped in early.
points: Leaders who stay disorganized about long-range deliverables lose the option to delegate once time pressure eliminates other people's availability to help.
Sorting tasks into today, this-week, and weeks/months-away buckets forces leaders to surface delegable sub-tasks before they become urgent.
Late delegation isn't just inefficient for the leader — it denies team members the learning and ownership that comes from early involvement.
quotes: A few days before the project that was once far away, you realize there was background, prep work, and other tasks that could have been done weeks ago to avoid having to rush it.
Because time is now of the essence, those who could have helped can no longer lend a hand.

Leaders who are overwhelmed by tasks, decisions, problems, and assignments typically focus on what they need to do and fail to chart out the steps needed for the many deliverables that are weeks or months away.
The best leaders create three distinct sets of tasks and priorities. Those that must be attended to today, those that need to be completed this week, and those that are weeks and months away.

By identifying the tasks that can be completed now, leaders have the option of delegating some or all of the steps to team members who have the capacity and desire to help and learn through the process.
